intro.text: The combat sport invented after every traditional martial art was declared legally incompatible with common sense.

Every five years, the Crown of Ten Thousand Fists gathered the finest fighters in the known world: mountain-temple prodigies, alleyway savants, discount-dojo champions, and masters of suspicious new disciplines such as Tactical Floor-Karate, Urban Noodle Defense, and Advanced Pointing. Each instructor promised their students could end a fight before the opponent finished laughing. The winner earned the Golden Gi, a lifetime supply of ceremonial noodles, and the right to correct strangers at parties.

By the first lunch break, the tournament had become less a test of martial discipline and more a public audit of bad decisions. Hidden weapons were found in sleeves, shoes, ceremonial fruit baskets, and one contestant’s emotional-support ferret. Three separate Grandmasters claimed that losing was proof their opponents had used forbidden cowardice. Judges accepted bribes in cash, coupons, and limited-edition protein powder. The flaming monks remain under active legal review.

The grand final ended when both finalists claimed the same trophy, the announcer was disarmed with a folding chair, and the ferret rang the victory bell for itself. One finalist immediately opened a seminar on why this proved he had won. The Council of Martial Arts Elders—three people in one robe, sharing one extremely judgmental pair of glasses—suspended the tournament before anyone could add ‘ferret champion’ to a résumé.

Their replacement was Paper-Fu: a new discipline with no bloodlines, no sacred prophecies, no shirtless nunchuck reviews, and exactly one rule that matters more than common sense. Advancement would be earned through combat, deckbuilding, increasingly unreasonable Belt Exams, and the sacred discipline of reading the card before yelling about it.

rows:
THE GOLDEN RULE
When a card directly contradicts this rulebook, the card wins. When two cards conflict, use the timing and priority rules in Section 15. When the table still cannot agree, the active player makes the temporary ruling, finishes the turn, and everyone may yell about it afterward.

intro.text: What Kind of Game Is This?

Dojo Deckbuilder is a competitive martial-arts deckbuilding game. Every player starts with the same awkward 15-card deck, plays cards to fight and generate Focus, buys stronger cards from a shared Market, equips deeply questionable gear, learns Combos, passes Belt Exams, and climbs from White Belt to Black Belt.
Fixed packs, not randomized boosters. Everyone knows what is in the box; nobody needs to sell a kidney for a foil raccoon.
Deckbuilding happens during play. Purchased Techniques and Items enter your discard pile and cycle into future hands; learned Combos remain face up beside your fighter.
Combat is direct. Attacks target High, Mid, or Low zones; defenders answer with cards, armor, and panic.
Two routes to victory. Reach Black Belt or become the last fighter standing.
Expandable by design. New dojos can add Characters, Techniques, Items, Equipment, Locations, Combos, Bosses, and new varieties of deeply avoidable nonsense.
Separate the decks now. Prevent the ritual sorting disaster later.

content.text: Character Cards — three fighters per player in Tag Team and Dojo Drama; one per player in Standard Clash or Quick Duel.

Fixed Starter Decks — every player uses the same 15 cards: Basic Jab, Basic Body Kick, Basic Shin Kick, Wild Swing, High Guard, Center Guard, Low Guard, Cover Up, Breathing Drill, Footwork Drill, and Bad Habit ×5.
Market Deck — shuffle all purchasable Attacks, Defenses, Katas, Items, Weapons, Armor, Consumables, and utility cards together. Reveal seven random cards; no card type is guaranteed a slot.
Combo Deck — a separate face-down deck. Combos never occupy Market slots and never enter a player's draw deck.
Location Deck — global battlefield conditions. One Location is active at a time; the fight can Scene Change during a round.
Boss Materials — three Boss Stage cards plus a dedicated 32-card Boss Arsenal Deck containing Attacks, Boss Guards, and Boss Techniques for Dojo Drama.
Trackers — tokens, cubes, dice, beads, tiny plastic fists, or suspiciously organized snacks for HP, XP, Focus, Tempo, promotion tasks, and temporary effects.
